title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: I'm Genevan by birth, and my family is one of the most prominent in the republic. My ancestors had been counselors and syndics — chief magistrates of Geneva — for many years. My father held several public positions with honor and a fine reputation. Everyone who knew him respected his integrity and his tireless dedication to public service. He spent his younger days constantly occupied by the affairs of his country. Various circumstances prevented him from marrying early, and it wasn't until late in life that he became a husband and father.

The story of his marriage says a great deal about his character, so I can't help telling it. One of his closest friends was a merchant named Beaufort who had fallen from prosperity into poverty through a series of misfortunes. Beaufort was a proud, unbending man who couldn't bear to live in poverty and obscurity in the same country where he'd once been distinguished for his wealth and status. After paying his debts honorably, he retreated with his daughter to the town of Lucerne, where he lived in hiding and wretchedness. My father loved Beaufort deeply and was devastated by his friend's retreat. He bitterly regretted the false pride that led his friend to behave so unworthily of their bond. He immediately set out to find him, hoping to persuade him to start over with his help and support.

Beaufort had hidden himself well. It took ten months before my father discovered where he was living. Overjoyed, he hurried to the house, which was on a poor street near the river Reuss. But when he entered, only misery and despair greeted him. Beaufort had saved only a tiny sum from his ruined fortune — enough to sustain him for a few months while he hoped to find respectable employment in a merchant's house. So the waiting was spent in idleness. His grief only deepened when he had time to think. Within three months, it had taken such a hold on his mind that he lay bedridden, unable to do anything.

His daughter cared for him with the greatest tenderness, but she watched in despair as their small fund shrank rapidly with no other source of income. But Caroline Beaufort had an uncommon spirit. Her courage rose to meet her adversity. She took on plain needlework. She braided straw. By various means, she managed to earn a pittance barely enough to keep them alive.

Several months passed this way. Her father grew worse. Her time was consumed entirely by nursing him. Her means of support dwindled. In the tenth month, her father died in her arms, leaving her an orphan and penniless. This final blow overwhelmed her. She was kneeling by Beaufort's coffin, weeping bitterly, when my father entered the room. He came like a guardian angel to the poor girl. She entrusted herself to his care. After burying his friend, he brought her to Geneva and placed her under the protection of a relative. Two years later, Caroline became his wife.

There was a considerable age difference between my parents, but this seemed only to draw them closer together. My father's strong sense of justice meant he had to deeply admire someone before he could deeply love them. Perhaps in earlier years he'd been hurt by discovering, too late, the unworthiness of someone he'd loved, which made him value proven character all the more. There was gratitude and devotion in his attachment to my mother, quite different from the doting fondness of old age. It was inspired by reverence for her virtues and a desire to somehow make up for the sorrows she'd endured. This gave a beautiful grace to his behavior toward her. Everything was arranged for her comfort and wishes. He sheltered her as a gardener shelters a delicate flower, protecting her from every harsh wind and surrounding her with everything that could bring pleasure to her gentle, generous heart. Her health, and even her once-steady spirit, had been shaken by what she'd been through. During the two years before their marriage, my father had gradually given up all his public duties. Immediately after their wedding, they traveled to Italy, seeking the pleasant climate and new experiences of that wonderful land to restore her weakened health.

From Italy they visited Germany and France. I, their eldest child, was born in Naples and traveled with them as an infant. For several years I was their only child. As attached as they were to each other, they seemed to draw inexhaustible stores of affection from a very mine of love to pour upon me. My mother's tender embraces and my father's warm, pleased smile are my earliest memories. I was their plaything and their idol — and something better: their child, the innocent, helpless creature given to them by heaven, whom they were to raise to be good, and whose future happiness or misery lay in their hands, depending on how well they fulfilled their duties toward me. With this deep awareness of what they owed to the being they had given life to, combined with the active tenderness that drove them both, every hour of my infancy was a lesson in patience, charity, and self-control. Yet I was guided so gently, as if by a silken cord, that it all felt like one continuous stream of happiness.

For a long time I was their only care. My mother had longed for a daughter, but I remained their only child. When I was about five, while traveling beyond the Italian border, they spent a week on the shores of Lake Como. Their generous natures often led them into the cottages of the poor. For my mother, this was more than a duty — it was a necessity, a passion. Remembering her own suffering and how she'd been helped, she felt compelled to be a guardian angel to the afflicted. During one of their walks, a poor cottage in a valley caught their attention. It looked especially wretched. The crowd of half-clothed children gathered around it spoke of poverty in its worst form. One day, when my father had gone to Milan alone, my mother visited this cottage with me. She found a peasant and his wife, hardworking and bent with care and labor, sharing a meager meal among five hungry children. Among them was one who drew my mother far more than all the rest. She seemed to be of different stock. The other four were dark-eyed, hardy little urchins. This child was thin and very fair. Her hair was the brightest living gold. Despite her poor clothing, it seemed to crown her with distinction. Her brow was clear and broad, her blue eyes cloudless, and her lips and features so expressive of warmth and sweetness that no one could look at her without seeing her as a being apart — heaven-sent, bearing a celestial mark in every feature.

The peasant woman, noticing my mother's wonder and admiration for this lovely girl, eagerly told her story. The child wasn't hers but the daughter of a Milanese nobleman. Her mother was German and had died giving birth to her. The baby had been placed with these good people to be nursed. They'd been better off then. They hadn't been long married, and their eldest child was just born. The girl's father was one of those Italians raised on memories of Italy's ancient glory — one of the schiavi ognor frementi — the "ever-chafing slaves" — who worked to win his country's freedom. He became a victim of its weakness. Whether he'd died or still languished in an Austrian dungeon, no one knew. His property was seized. His child became an orphan and a beggar. She continued living with her foster parents and bloomed in their rough home, fairer than a garden rose among dark brambles.

When my father returned from Milan, he found a child playing with me in the hall of our villa — a child fairer than any painted angel, a creature who seemed to radiate light, whose form and movements were lighter than those of a chamois, the nimble wild goat of the hills. The mystery was soon explained. With his permission, my mother persuaded the foster parents to give the child to her. They were fond of the sweet orphan. Her presence had been a blessing to them. But it would be unfair to keep her in poverty when God had provided such powerful protection. They consulted their village priest. The result was that Elizabeth Lavenza became a member of my parents' household — more than my sister — the beautiful and adored companion of all my interests and pleasures.

Everyone loved Elizabeth. The passionate, almost reverential devotion everyone felt for her, which I shared, became my pride and delight. The evening before she was brought to our home, my mother had said playfully, "I have a pretty present for my Victor — tomorrow he shall have it." And when, the next morning, she presented Elizabeth to me as her promised gift, I — with childish seriousness — took her words literally and looked upon Elizabeth as mine. Mine to protect, love, and cherish. Every compliment paid to her, I received as praise of my own treasure. We called each other cousin. But no word could capture the bond between us — she was more than a sister, for until death she was to be mine alone.
